newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: ANALYSTS WARN C/A DEFICIT MAY SHOW LACK OF REFORM.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS WARN C/A DEFICIT MAY SHOW LACK OF REFORM.

text.p: Slovak economists on Monday said short-term capital inflows were propping up the country's balance of payments, and warned that insufficient economic restructuring may exacerbate a growing current account deficit.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) released figures on Monday showing the current account had swung to a deficit for the first 11 months of 1996 of $1.4 billion, compared with a $480.6 million surplus for the same period in 1995.

And while a capital account surplus of $1.57 billion for the same period was enough to cover the shortfall, analysts said net short-term capital, which can flow out as fast as it comes in, accounted for more than half of the figure.
"We appear to be out of the woods for the time being, but it is a problem for the future," Martin Barto, an analyst with ING Barings, told Reuters.
"The current account deficit is covered largely with short-term flows, which are a source of danger," he added.
Once the engine of economic growth in Slovakia, exports have waned as an economic slowdown in the West has bit hard into the low value-added products it traditionally produces.

Slovakia posted a foreign trade shortfall of 64.54 billion crowns for the whole of 1996, compared with a 5.69 billion crown deficit for January-December 1995. This, in turn, forced the central bank to revise its current account forecast from a slight surplus to a deficit of $610-$965 million.

Ivan Miklos, an economist with MESA 10 Group, said the continual current account and trade deficits will put pressure on the state's foreign currency reserves, and could prompt the government to take action to limit imports.
"Sooner or later, reserves will be on line. This problem may be temporarily delayed but this just multiplies the effects...the economy's problem is insufficient industrial reform," he said.
The NBS's hard currency reserves firmed to $3.473 billion to December 31, from $3.424 billion at the beginning of 1996, but they now cover only 3.4 months of country's imports down from 4.0 months.

"It (the deficit) may worsen in December, it will be further covered with loans judging by the NBS's stable reserves...but the situation suggests the government may tap some kind of foreign trade regulation," Barto said.
Despite its being heavily-criticised for its hostile political climate, Slovakia has been one of the strongest economies of the former East Bloc.

GDP growth, boosted by credit-driven domestic demand, rose a real 7.0 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 1996, after a 7.4 percent growth in 1995. Its inflation rate remains at a region-low of 5.4 percent.

But its key M2 money supply, buoyed by domestic lending, Slovakia's key money supply measure, M2, rose 15.7 percent for 1996, forcing the central bank to implement a series of tightening measures to curb loan expansion.

"It is necessary to closely adhere to the NBS's monetary programme, because the economy is not performing well enough to keep imports at the current pace, to export more is impossible," Pavol Karasz, head of Economics Institute at the Slovak Academy of Science, said.
